slides.title: Construction Problems and Field Extensions
slides.notes: Open the lecture by naming the chapter's shift in viewpoint: a construction problem is also a field-entry problem. The familiar tools of straightedge and compass are not merely physical restrictions; they control which coordinates can be obtained. Emphasize that the printed span 241-294 and PDF pages 253-306 cover both famous impossibility results and a few surprising positive constructions.

slides.title: Chapter Route
slides.notes: Use the route slide to separate the lecture into four acts. First we translate constructions into coordinate fields, then we test the three classical problems, then we study the regular 17-gon as a success story, and finally we widen the toolbox with a marked ruler. This framing helps students see why a chapter about constructions ends with finite extensions and Galois-order diagnostics.

slides.title: The Field Ledger
slides.notes: Stress that the ledger is a bookkeeping device for coordinates, not a recipe for drawing every line. Starting from rational data, line-line intersections use field arithmetic and circle intersections add at most a square root. The important invariant is multiplicative: a tower built from quadratic gates has total degree a power of two.

slides.title: Three Classical Requests
slides.notes: Present the famous problems as three different algebraic failure modes. Doubling the cube and trisecting a general angle already fail because a cubic degree appears where only powers of two are allowed. Squaring the circle is even farther away because the needed relation involves pi, and the obstruction is transcendence rather than just an odd algebraic degree.

slides.title: Angle Trisection as a Cubic
slides.notes: Walk through the cosine identity as a bridge between a geometric request and an algebraic test. If a 60 degree angle were trisected by straightedge and compass, then the associated cosine value would live in a quadratic tower. The cubic relation is a compact way to see the obstruction without drawing a complicated failed construction.

slides.title: Quadratic Towers as a Filter
slides.notes: The tree visual should be read from left to right: each compass-level choice splits a field by degree at most two. A number may have a minimal polynomial of degree four or eight and still pass this first filter, but degree three cannot pass. Mention that the filter is necessary in this general form, and in several chapter examples it becomes decisive once irreducibility is checked.

slides.title: Regular Polygons Become Cyclotomic
slides.notes: Shift from impossibility to classification by regular polygons. The vertices are roots of unity, so the algebraic question is controlled by the cyclotomic field rather than by a single ad hoc diagram. For straightedge and compass, the relevant group size must have only the prime two in its degree signal.

slides.title: Why the 17-gon Is Special
slides.notes: For the regular 17-gon, the real coordinate 2 cos(2 pi over 17) has degree eight, which is 2 cubed. That degree alone does not draw the polygon, but it opens the door to a tower of quadratic choices. The nested period boxes in the visual show how a complicated root-of-unity orbit can be repeatedly split in half.

slides.title: A Degree Test Is Not the Whole Story
slides.notes: Pause here to prevent a common misconception. Degree equal to a power of two is a strong signal, but arbitrary algebraic numbers require more than the minimal degree alone; the behavior of conjugates and the splitting field can still matter. The slide's warning prepares students for the later quartic example whose root field and splitting field tell different stories.

slides.title: Marked Ruler: A New Gate
slides.notes: Introduce the marked ruler as a controlled enlargement of the construction language. A neusis step slides a fixed marked distance until two incidence conditions are met, and that motion hides a conchoid-type curve. The key contrast is that the added move can encode cubic and quartic behavior that compass-only constructions cannot reach.

slides.title: The Conchoid Hidden in Neusis
slides.notes: Use the diagram as a moving-constraint picture rather than a static finished construction. The marked segment forces a fixed distance while one endpoint lies on a line and the other endpoint targets a ray or second line. Eliminating the sliding parameter produces a quartic intersection problem, which is exactly the algebraic door the chapter wants to open.

slides.title: Cubic Equations Enter the Geometry
slides.notes: Connect the earlier trisection obstruction to the new marked-ruler power. The same cubic shape that blocked straightedge and compass can be attacked once angle trisection or an equivalent neusis move is admitted. This is not magic; it is a controlled addition of a new algebraic operation to the field ledger.

slides.title: Quartics via a Cubic Resolvent
slides.notes: The quartic route should be read as a dependency graph rather than as a formula to memorize. Solving a quartic can be organized by reducing part of the problem to a cubic resolvent and then finishing with square-root choices. This fits the chapter's theme: construction rules are best understood by the field operations they authorize.

slides.title: Finite Extensions: Root Field vs Splitting Field
slides.notes: This slide distinguishes two degrees that students often merge. A single root can generate a degree-four extension while the full collection of roots may live in a larger splitting field. For construction questions, that larger symmetry can reveal obstructions or permissions that the minimal polynomial degree by itself might conceal.

slides.title: Polygon Filter Lab
slides.notes: Summarize the notebook lab as a reproducible computational check. For regular n-gons, Euler's phi function gives the cyclotomic degree signal, so compass construction passes when the relevant prime content is only two. With a marked ruler, powers of two and three are allowed in this simplified polygon filter, giving examples such as the 9-gon that were not compass-only.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter's central sentence: construction tools are algebraic tools in disguise. Straightedge and compass build quadratic towers; the 17-gon succeeds because its real cyclotomic data descends through such a tower; marked rulers add cubic and quartic gates. The final lesson is methodological as much as factual: ask which field extension a geometric demand is asking you to enter.
